title: The Complete Story of Yue Fei
subtitle: Thirty Years of Fame and Glory Are but Dust and Earth · Eight Thousand Li of Cloud and Moon
description: The Complete Story of Yue Fei is a full-length heroic legend compiled by the Qing-dynasty writer Qian Cai and expanded by Jin Feng, comprising eighty chapters. Centered on Yue Fei's campaigns against the Jin dynasty — from his birth to his martyrdom at the Stormy Pavilion, and then to Yue Lei's northern campaign — the maternal precept of "utmost loyalty in serving the state" runs throughout. The novel created such household figures as Yue Fei, Yue Yun, Niu Gao, and Jin Wushu, and remains one of the most beloved patriotic legends in Chinese folk culture.

route.title: The Complete Story of Yue Fei: Utmost Loyalty in Serving the State — A Hero's Road That Stirs Mountains and Rivers
route.intro:
My hair bristles beneath my helmet, I lean against the railing as the drizzling rain ceases. Lifting my eyes, I let out a long roar at the sky — my ardent feelings violent and intense. Thirty years of fame and glory are but dust and earth; eight thousand li of cloud and moon.
Qian Cai (dates unknown), style name Jinwen, was a native of Renhe, Zhejiang. He lived in the Kangxi reign of the early Qing dynasty, an age when "overthrow the Qing and restore the Ming" was already a thing of the past, but the pain of national subjugation had not yet healed in the hearts of Han Chinese scholars. With passionate fervor and profound sorrow, he wrote The Complete Story of Yue Fei. Yue Fei's story has long belonged not only to the Southern Song but has been etched into every Chinese person's collective imagination of loyalty and righteousness. Let us follow in Yue Fei's footsteps — from his hometown in Tangyin to the Yue Fei Temple in Hangzhou, from the great victory at Zhuxian Town to the final regret at the Stormy Pavilion — visiting the national heritage sites that bear witness to the spirit of serving the state with utmost loyalty.

stops.title: Stop One: Tangyin · The Roc Takes Flight
stops.content: In the second year of Chongning, Northern Song (1103 AD), Yue Fei was born into a farming family in Tangyin, Xiangzhou. It is said that at his birth, a giant roc flew over the roof, hence his given name Fei (to soar) and his courtesy name Pengju (roc ascendant). Though poor, he was diligent in his studies as a youth. His mother, Lady Yao, tattooed four characters — "尽忠报国" (serve the state with utmost loyalty) — into his back. These four words were carved into Yue Fei's very bones and blood, and into the soul of the Chinese people for over eight hundred years to come. Today, the Tangyin Yue Fei Temple stands on his native soil. First built in the first year of Jingtai, Ming (1450 AD), it includes a mountain gate, a main hall, a Wise Mother Shrine, and numerous stelae. Entering the temple, the first thing you see are the kneeling statues of Qin Hui and four other traitors — from the very beginning in his hometown, the distinction between loyalty and treachery is drawn in stark lines. The statue of Yue Fei in the main hall is imposing and dignified; a plaque bearing the four characters "还我河山" (Return Our Rivers and Mountains) hangs high above, as if this hero had never left, forever guarding the beloved land of his home. The Tangyin Yue Fei Temple is laid out with complete solemnity. The plaque over the mountain gate, "Temple of the Loyal King Yue of Song," was inscribed in the Ming dynasty. Within, the Jingzhong Archway, the mountain gate, the main hall, the Wise Mother Shrine, and the Filial Daughter Shrine unfold in sequence. The main hall is five bays wide, with a hip-and-gable roof covered in green glazed tiles. Inside, Yue Fei's statue sits upright in golden armor and purple robes, a sword at his side, the cross-board bearing "还我河山" — four characters of such mighty brushwork that they pierce straight to the heart. In the Wise Mother Shrine, the statue of Lady Yao sits with gentle dignity, calling to mind the legend of the mother's tattoo. Those four words were not tattooed only on Yue Fei's back — they were branded into the collective memory of an entire nation. The Complete Story of Yue Fei writes that a giant roc flew over at Yue Fei's birth — this is, of course, a legend, but the Chinese people choose to believe it, because we need our heroes to have a heavenly mandate, a grand beginning to explain a life of extraordinary deed. The novel also depicts Yue Fei's teacher, a martial arts master named Zhou Tong — the same man who trained Lin Chong and Lu Junyi in Water Margin. Zhou Tong took Yue Fei as his disciple at Mount Lishui, teaching him the eighteen martial arts and military strategy. Though much of this is fictional embellishment, the farming village of Tangyin did produce a boy named Yue Fei who, with sheer courage and a pure heart, rose from an ordinary soldier to a field marshal — a true story more remarkable than any novel.

stops.title: Stop Two: Kaifeng · The Defense of the Eastern Capital
stops.content: After the Jingkang Incident, the Northern Song fell and the iron hooves of the Jin cavalry trampled the Eastern Capital. Yue Fei joined the army and distinguished himself repeatedly in battle, rising from a common soldier to a commander of thousands upon thousands of troops. In the Kaifeng region, he smashed the Jin forces many times. Wherever the banner of the "Yue Family Army" appeared, the Jin troops fled in panic — "It is easier to shake a mountain than to shake the Yue Family Army!" The Xiangguo Temple in Kaifeng is a landmark that appears many times in The Complete Story of Yue Fei. In the Northern Song, the Great Xiangguo Temple was a bustling center where envoys from ten thousand states came to pay homage. Yue Fei's story unfolds in the darkest hour of this ancient capital's fall from its peak. The temple's bell has pierced through the smoke of war and through eight hundred years of time — come here, and you can still see the Song-dynasty style of the halls and the unceasing devotion of the incense-bearers. Every inch of Kaifeng's soil is steeped in the prosperity of the Northern Song and the grief of a nation lost. It was on this very land that Yue Fei swore his oath: "Let us drive straight to the Yellow Dragon Palace!" The history of the Xiangguo Temple is itself a stirring epic. First built in the sixth year of Tianbao, Northern Qi (555 AD), it was originally called Jianguo Temple, then renamed Great Xiangguo Temple by Tang Ruizong after a dream. It reached its zenith in the Northern Song — covering five hundred and forty mu, governing sixty-four Chan and Vinaya cloisters, it was the largest imperial temple in the Eastern Capital. When Yue Fei served in the military at Kaifeng as a young man, he must have seen this great temple in its glory — "gold and azure dazzling, clouds and rainbows paling in comparison," as contemporary records describe the Xiangguo Temple's halls. Chapters Four through Ten of The Complete Story of Yue Fei detail his military career in Kaifeng. Starting as a reconnaissance scout, he repeatedly distinguished himself under the command of Marshal Zong Ze. The most thrilling passage is "Yue Fei Unseats the Young King Liang" — the arrogant Chai Gui (a descendant of the Later Zhou imperial house) was knocked off his horse in a martial tournament by Yue Fei's spear. Though this is fictional, it reflects the folk imagination of Yue Fei: not only the embodiment of loyalty, but also of courage and skill. The bells of the Great Xiangguo Temple have rung for a thousand years unbroken — those morning bells and evening drums have pierced through the splendor of Bianliang and through the national shame of the Jingkang Incident, and they still ring today.

stops.title: Stop Three: Zhuxian Town · The Great Rout of the Golden Dragon Formation
stops.content: In the tenth year of Shaoxing (1140 AD), after crushing the Jin forces at Yancheng and Yingchang, Yue Fei pressed his advantage and drove straight to Zhuxian Town outside Kaifeng. Here, with five hundred of his elite Beiwei troops, he shattered the hundred-thousand-strong army of Jin Wushu — the Golden Dragon Formation, the Iron Pagoda heavy cavalry, the Guaizi Ma horse-armored units — all the Jin's trump cards collapsed before the Yue Family Army. Yue Fei said to his men: "Let us drink together when we reach the Yellow Dragon Palace!" But just as victory was within reach, the imperial court issued twelve golden tokens in rapid succession, ordering him back to the capital. Yue Fei looked up to heaven and sighed: "Ten years of effort, destroyed in a single day!" Today, the Zhuxian Town Yue Fei Temple (including the Lord Guan Temple) stands on this ancient battlefield where triumph turned to defeat. The temple has a mountain gate, a main hall, and inscribed stelae — every stele is a later generation's unwilling question: if those twelve golden tokens had never come, how would history have been rewritten? The Zhuxian Town Yue Fei Temple (including the Lord Guan Temple) was built in the fourteenth year of Chenghua, Ming (1478 AD). Together with the Yue Fei temples in Tangyin, Wuchang, and Hangzhou, it is one of the four great Yue Fei temples in China. Before the temple stand five iron kneeling statues of the traitors — one more than at the Hangzhou temple — the fifth being Wang Diao, a subordinate of the general Zhang Jun who helped frame Yue Fei. The statue of Yue Fei in the main hall is not in the usual military garb — he wears the robes of a civil official and holds a book, because the people of Zhuxian Town wanted to commemorate not General Yue Fei, but the scholar who was recalled by those twelve golden tokens with a heart full of indignation. The passage describing the "Great Rout of the Golden Dragon Formation" in The Complete Story of Yue Fei is brilliantly written. Jin Wushu deployed the formation, "a thousand troops and ten thousand horsemen formed into a single dragon." Yue Fei ordered Yue Yun, Zhang Xian, Niu Gao, and others to charge in from four directions, striking at the dragon's weakest points. The novel says: "This great battle darkened heaven and earth, blotting out the sun and moon." In the actual Battle of Yancheng, Yue Fei used long-handled scythes to break the Jin Guaizi Ma — targeting the horses' legs, so that one fallen horse would bring down the whole unit. Zhuxian Town was one step from "driving straight to the Yellow Dragon Palace." Those twelve golden tokens turned that step into the longest distance in Chinese history.

buildings.n: Yuefei Temple in Zhuxian Town (including Guandi Temple)

stops.title: Stop Four: Wuchang · Gazing Toward the Central Plains from the Yellow Crane Tower
stops.content: Yue Fei stationed his troops in Wuchang several times in his life, using it as a rear base for his northern campaigns. Climbing the Yellow Crane Tower and looking north toward the Central Plains, he poured out the immortal River All Red — "The shame of Jingkang is still unavenged; the hatred of a subject — when will it end!" Every line is blood and fire erupting from the depths of his heart. Within the Yellow Crane Tower Park on the banks of the Yangtze River in Wuhan stands the Yuan-dynasty Shengxiang Pagoda. This stone-built, bowl-shaped pagoda, over nine meters tall, is a rare example of Yuan-dynasty Tibetan Buddhist stupa architecture in the middle reaches of the Yangtze. Though built a century after Yue Fei's death, it stands silently before the Yellow Crane Tower, watching the rolling Yangtze flow eastward — just as Yue Fei wrote in River All Red: "Let us drive our chariots to trample the Gap of Helan." Only the ten-thousand-li Yangtze can match this fervent loyalty and indignation. The Shengxiang Pagoda is one of the oldest above-ground structures in Wuhan, built in the third year of Zhizheng, Yuan (1343 AD). It is a masonry bowl-shaped pagoda, standing 9.34 meters tall — a Sumeru throne base, a bowl-shaped body, thirteen rings of the chhatra umbrella, and a bronze jewel spire. This is a classic Tibetan Buddhist lama pagoda, extremely rare in the middle and lower Yangtze region. The pagoda body is carved with Sanskrit mantras and Buddha images, still legible after nearly seven hundred years of wind and rain. The Wuhan of Yue Fei's time was not the Wuhan of today. In the Southern Song, Ezhou (Wuchang) was the key military stronghold of the middle Yangtze. Yue Fei made it his headquarters for seven years. Was River All Red written at the Yellow Crane Tower? Academics debate it, but the common people believe it was. "My hair bristles, I lean against the railing as the drizzling rain ceases" — standing on the Yellow Crane Tower, leaning on the railing and gazing at the Yangtze, that desolate and stirring passion naturally wells up. Yue Fei spent his entire life on the road to "restoring the rivers and mountains." The Beiwei troops he so carefully trained were among the most formidable cavalry in the world — "men in heavy armor, horses with iron trappings." What a tragedy that this invincible force could never be used on the battlefield of recovering the Central Plains.

stops.title: Stop Five: Hangzhou · The Unfounded Crime at the Stormy Pavilion
stops.content: After Yue Fei was recalled to Lin'an, Qin Hui sent him to prison on the charge of "moyou you" — "perhaps there is such an offense." On the twenty-ninth day of the twelfth month of the eleventh year of Shaoxing (January 27, 1142), Yue Fei was killed at the Stormy Pavilion of the Supreme Court in Hangzhou, at the age of thirty-nine. Before the execution, he wrote eight large characters on his deposition: "Heaven's sun shines bright, Heaven's sun shines bright!" Twenty years later, the injustice was redressed, and his remains were reinterred at the southern foot of Qixia Ridge by West Lake. Today, the Tomb of Yue Fei (Yue Fei Temple) is one of the most sacred places in the Chinese heart. Before the tomb stand a screen wall, a spirit-way, and gate-towers — the circular tomb mound bears the tablet "Tomb of the Prince of E of Song," flanked by stone figures and stone horses standing eternal guard. Four iron kneeling statues of traitors face the tomb forever — Qin Hui, Lady Wang, Moqi Xie, and Zhang Jun. For eight hundred years, every visitor who has come to pay homage has had to make their own choice between loyalty and treachery: to die standing like Yue Fei, or to live kneeling like Qin Hui. Every detail of the Tomb of Yue Fei is rich with symbolism. The tomb complex comprises the spirit-way, the tomb mound, and the Loyalty Shrine. The stone figures lining the spirit-way — three pairs of attendants and horses, sheep, and tigers — were finely carved during the Ming reconstruction: the stone tiger's mane can be counted strand by strand, the stone figures' robe folds are natural and flowing. The Loyalty Shrine is the main structure of the complex, with a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof. Inside, Yue Fei's statue wears a general's helmet, purple robes, and golden armor, with his right hand clenched in a fist, his left hand on his sword, his eyes blazing like torches. On the walls of the shrine are four characters carved in stone, the work of Ming-dynasty Zhejiang official Hong Zhu: "尽忠报国" — but the character "国" is deliberately missing a stroke, meaning "the national territory has not yet been recovered." When The Complete Story of Yue Fei writes of the Stormy Pavilion, the tone is one of extreme bitterness. Before being strangled, Yue wrote on the wall of his cell: "Heaven's sun shines bright, Heaven's sun shines bright." Qin Hui sent two jailers to carry out the execution. Yue Fei bowed three times toward heaven and met his death with composure. It is said that on that day, the sky over Hangzhou was covered with dark clouds, and West Lake sobbed — as if Heaven itself were weeping. These details are, of course, embellishments added by later generations. But eight hundred years later, when you stand in the Yue Fei Temple before those four iron kneeling statues, the simple justice of "everyone may spit on them" still burns hot.

stops.title: Stop Six: Hangzhou · The Green Hills Are Blessed to Hold the Hero's Bones
stops.content: Yue Fei's martyrdom is the most heartbreaking climax of The Complete Story of Yue Fei, but his spirit did not perish with the end of his life. The tale of Yue Lei's northern campaign spread widely among the people — it was the common folk using their imagination to write a "happy ending" for their hero. Though the course of history could not be changed, the people's hearts rendered their own verdict. In Hangzhou, beyond the Yue Fei Temple, the mountains and waters of Qixia Ridge are also steeped in the hero's spirit. Whenever the autumn wind rustles and West Lake ripples, the people naturally think of Yue Fei and his River All Red. And the Liuhe Pagoda stands silent watch by the Qiantang River — "The green hills are blessed to hold the hero's bones; the white iron is innocent that was cast into kneeling traitors." Over eight hundred years have passed, yet the incense before Yue Fei's tomb has never ceased. A man executed on the charge of "perhaps" has become an inextinguishable spiritual torch in the Chinese heart — that, perhaps, is history's most righteous judgment.
